faq.title: Frequently Asked [[Questions]]
faq.a1: Medical Cost-Sharing is a community-based model where members voluntarily pool resources to help cover each other's approved medical expenses. When a member has an eligible medical bill, the community shares the cost among all active members, making healthcare more accessible and affordable.
faq.q2: How is We Kongsi different from insurance?
faq.a2: We Kongsi is NOT an insurance product. Unlike insurance, We Kongsi is a community-driven program where members help members — there's no insurance company taking profit. Members contribute only when there are approved medical cases, making it more transparent and community-focused.
faq.q3: How much do I contribute monthly?
faq.a3: Your monthly sharing depends on the approved medical cases that month, divided among all active members. Inpatient sharing is capped at RM60 per member. With the COB option you may contribute an additional RM15. The membership fee is separate and fixed at RM40/month (or RM100/quarter, RM360/year).
faq.q4: What happens if there are no approved cases?
faq.a4: If there are no approved hospital cases in a month, no inpatient sharing is required. Your Sharing Account balance is carried forward and remains available for future months when the community needs support.
faq.a5: COB provides support for everyday illnesses, including telemedicine via HEYDOC Health and clinic visits at MiCare panel clinics nationwide. Members receive up to RM120 support per episode, for up to 8 episodes per year, covering 17 eligible outpatient conditions.
faq.q6: Can I opt out of COB?
faq.a6: Yes, COB is optional. You can choose an Inpatient-Only package without COB, or include COB for comprehensive outpatient support. Speak to your We Kongsi agent for details on the available options.
faq.q7: How does sharing work in practice?
faq.a7: Each month, all approved medical bills are totalled and divided equally among active members. For example, if RM200,000 in bills is approved across 5,000 active members, each member shares RM40 that month. Inpatient sharing is always capped at RM60/month.
faq.q8: How do I join We Kongsi?
faq.a8: Membership is taken out through a referrer, so there is no sign-up form to fill in on your own. Chat with us and we will connect you with one — they will take you through the plans, check you are eligible and complete the registration with you.

flow.title:

[[Contributions]] Flow
flow.desc: We Kongsi separates the money that runs the programme from the money that shares medical costs. The funds set aside for sharing belong to members and are held independently — We Kongsi never holds or controls them.

s1.d: A separate membership fee runs the programme, while your Sharing Account contribution funds the actual sharing of eligible medical costs. Both are collected by auto-debit eMandate through our payments partner, Curlec.

s2.d: Money set aside for sharing sits in a member-owned Sharing Account held and managed by a licensed Trustee, Palladium. We Kongsi has no access to it — the Sharing Account belongs to the members.

s3.d: When a member has an eligible hospital or outpatient cost, the community shares it. Each verified case is published openly, and the agreed amount is shared from the pool — directly supporting the member in need.

flow.note: We Kongsi operates on a **no-profit sharing model** — funds set aside for sharing are used only to support members' eligible medical costs, never to generate profit for the company.

wsq.title: WeShare, [[Answered]].
wsq.lede: The short answers. The Program Guidelines above carry the full detail.

join.label: Joining
join.a1: Members are Malaysians living in the country, aged 5 to 45 and healthy on the day they enrol, with no restriction by ethnicity or religion. The account itself is opened by someone 18 or over.
join.a2: Yes. One account can hold several members, each enrolled individually and each meeting the same entry age and health requirement. The account owner manages them all — details, payments and support run through the one account.
join.q3: What do I need to join?
join.a3: You need to be 18 or over to open the account. Have your NRIC, a mobile number, an email address and a few minutes for the health screening questionnaire ready — a referrer completes the registration with you.

pay.label: What you pay
pay.q1: What exactly am I paying for?
pay.a1: Two things. A membership fee that runs the programme, and a contribution to your own Sharing Account that goes towards members' approved medical costs.
pay.q2: How much is the membership fee?
pay.a2: RM40 a month, RM100 a quarter or RM360 a year. Paying quarterly or annually costs less over a year.
pay.q3: How much is deducted for sharing?
pay.a3: Never more than RM60 a month, deducted on the 7th. In a month with no approved cases, nothing is deducted at all.

wait.label: Waiting periods
wait.a1: Accidental injury is covered from day one, up to RM10,000. Common illnesses become eligible after 90 days, and specified illnesses such as diabetes, heart conditions and cancer after 180 days.
wait.q2: What about conditions I already have?
wait.a2: Anything that existed before you joined is not eligible to share. Conditions are disclosed through the health screening when you enrol.

share.label: Sharing & co-share
share.a1: Up to RM1,000,000 of eligible inpatient costs a year, and the limit renews every 12 months.
share.q2: Do I pay part of the bill myself?
share.a2: Yes, a co-share — 10% for ages 6 to 45, 25% under 6 and 20% from 46 upwards, capped at RM500 per admission.
share.q3: How do I know bills are fair?
share.a3: Every approved bill is reviewed against the MMA 13th Schedule of Fees, the recognised benchmark for medical charges in Malaysia.

care.label: When you need care
care.q1: What do I do when I need treatment?
care.a1: Start with a teleconsultation through HEYDOC. If you need more, a clinic visit is arranged, and the doctor refers you to a panel hospital when hospital care is required.
care.a2: Get treated first. You never need approval before emergency care — just tell us as soon as you reasonably can afterwards.

stop.label: Pausing & leaving
stop.q1: What if I miss a payment?
stop.a1: Your membership is suspended and benefits pause. You have 26 days to settle before it is terminated.
stop.q2: Can I get my money back if I leave?
stop.a2: The balance in your Sharing Account is yours and is refunded when you leave. Membership fees already paid are not refunded.

wcq.title: WeCare, [[Answered]].
wcq.lede: The short answers. The Program Guidelines above carry the full detail.

basics.label: The basics
basics.a1: A subscription for everyday outpatient care — a doctor on the phone whenever you need one, plus an allowance for medicine and clinic visits. It is not insurance, Takaful or a medical card.
basics.a2: Any Malaysian living in the country. There is no age limit, no health declaration and no health screening.
basics.a3: No. Cover starts the moment payment is confirmed.

episodes.label: Care Episodes
episodes.a1: The unit WeCare is counted in. Every quarter you get one Medicine Episode and one Clinic Visit Episode — one of each, not two of either.
episodes.a2: Only when treatment is actually given: medicine dispensed, or a visit to a panel clinic. Speaking to a doctor is free and uses none.
episodes.q3: What if I do not use them?
episodes.a3: They stay available for the rest of the subscription year, up to a balance of eight. They do not carry into the next year.

using.label: Using it
using.q1: How do I see a doctor?
using.a1: Open the MiCare MyMed app and describe the problem. Teleconsultation runs daily from 9am to 10pm, including weekends and public holidays — unlimited and free.
using.q2: Can I just go to a clinic?
using.a2: Yes. Walk into a participating panel GP clinic, cashless, with no referral and no phone call first.
using.a3: Collected from a participating pharmacy or delivered to you, nationwide.

covered.label: What's covered
covered.q1: What does the RM40 cap mean?
covered.a1: Each Care Episode is supported up to RM40, covering the consultation, the medicine and its delivery. Anything above that is yours to pay, and you are always told before it happens.
covered.a2: Hospitalisation, specialist care, chronic conditions and repeat prescriptions, scans, screening, vaccinations, and non-medical items such as vitamins.
covered.q3: What if I have an emergency?
covered.a3: Go straight to the nearest clinic or hospital. WeCare is for everyday outpatient care, not emergencies.

pay.label: Paying & stopping
pay.a1: RM45 a quarter or RM160 a year, paid in advance. There is no registration fee and no administration fee.
pay.q2: What if a payment is late?
pay.a2: Cover pauses and you have 26 days to settle. Paying inside that window restores everything immediately.
pay.q3: Can I stop and come back?
pay.a3: Yes, at any time, with no waiting period and no health declaration. A RM30 reactivation fee applies.

about.label: About We Kongsi
about.a1: A community medical cost-sharing programme. Members contribute to their own Sharing Account, and when someone has an approved medical need, the cost is shared across the community rather than carried alone.
about.a2: No. Nothing is underwritten and no risk is transferred to a company. For protection beyond what the community shares, speak to a licensed insurer or Takaful operator.
about.a3: The programme is open to all Malaysians living in the country, of any ethnicity or religion, and is developed with Afsha Shariah Advisory.

plans.label: The two plans
plans.q1: What is the difference between WeShare and WeCare?
plans.a1: WeShare shares the cost of hospitalisation — the big, rare bill. WeCare covers everyday outpatient care — the doctor, the medicine and the clinic visit.
plans.a2: They answer different problems, and many members take both. Each plan page sets out exactly what it does and does not do.
plans.a3: Yes. They are separate plans, with separate payments and separate rules.

join.label: Joining
join.a1: WeShare members are aged 5 to 45 and healthy on the day they enrol. WeCare has no age limit and no health screening. Both are open to Malaysians living in the country, and the account is opened by someone 18 or over, who can enrol family members under it.
join.a2: Through a referrer. Chat with us and we will put you in touch with one, who will go through the plans with you and complete your registration.
join.a3: WeCare starts the moment payment is confirmed. WeShare phases in, with accidental injury covered from day one.

money.label: Money
money.a1: WeShare is RM40 a month, RM100 a quarter or RM360 a year, plus a sharing contribution capped at RM60 a month. WeCare is RM45 a quarter or RM160 a year.
money.a2: By auto-debit, set up with our payment partner Curlec when you join.
money.a3: Your WeShare Sharing Account balance is yours and is refunded when you leave. Fees already paid are not refunded.

trust.label: Trust & transparency
trust.a1: Your Sharing Account is held by Palladium Trustee, a licensed trustee company. We Kongsi has no access to it.
trust.q2: How do I know what I am sharing?
trust.a2: Every shareable case is published on the 7th of each month, before anything is deducted. The monthly report is on this site.
trust.q3: Do I have to take part in every case?
trust.a3: No. Taking part is voluntary, and you may leave during the publishing period rather than share in a case you object to.

help.label: Getting help
help.q1: Who do I call about a hospital admission?
help.a1: e-MAS, on 03-9213 0103. They handle everything inpatient — the hospital panel, admissions, guarantee letters and anything at the hospital counter.
help.q2: Who do I call about everyday care?
help.a2: MiCare, on 1800 88 7940. They handle everything outpatient — the MyMed app, teleconsultation, panel clinic visits and medicine — for WeCare and for the WeShare outpatient add-on.
help.q3: Who do I contact about my account?
help.a3: We Kongsi customer service, for registration, payment, membership status and anything about the membership itself.

kongsisihat.d: A community health day at NU Sentral — free health screenings, healthcare awareness activities and volunteers from across the community, open to everyone.
kongsisihat.alt: Volunteers, partners and the We Kongsi team at Kongsi Sihat, NU Sentral
kongsisihat.alt2: The HEAL Carnival stage — Health, Empowerment, Awareness, Lifestyle
body: In October 2025, We Kongsi organised Kongsi Sihat at the NU Sentral Centre Court, bringing free health screenings and healthcare awareness activities into a place where people were already passing through. The event ran from 10:00am to 6:00pm and was open to the public.
Kongsi Sihat was supported by e-MAS, JCI Kuala Lumpur, the Blockchain for Good Alliance and MASVERSE, alongside volunteers from across the community. Membership was not required to take part.
## Meeting People Where They Already Are
Most people do not skip a health check because they have decided against it. They skip it because it means taking time off work, finding a clinic, waiting to be seen and paying for the visit.

Removing those barriers changes the outcome. A screening table in a shopping centre is not a clinical breakthrough, but it addresses the practical obstacles that keep many people from having a basic check at all.
## Why Prevention Matters to a Cost-Sharing Community

Every approved case in the monthly sharing report represents a medical cost the community carries together. A morning of screening and health advice costs considerably less than the hospital admission it may help to avoid — for the individual, and for everyone who shares with them.

A community medical cost-sharing programme therefore has a genuine interest in its members staying well. Health awareness is not a secondary activity alongside the programme; it supports the sustainability of the programme itself.
## Open to Members and Non-Members Alike
It would have been simpler to hold a members-only event. Kongsi Sihat was opened to anyone who walked past instead.

A health screening is valuable to the person receiving it regardless of whether they ever join a programme, and healthcare awareness is most useful when it reaches people who have not yet thought about it. The event was built around that principle.
## Bringing the Community Together
There is a second outcome from an event like this that is harder to record in a report.

A medical cost-sharing programme is, in structure, several thousand people who have agreed to help one another with hospital bills. That agreement works because people take it seriously, and it is easier to take seriously once members, staff, partners and volunteers have spent a day together doing something useful.
Kongsi Sihat gave the community a place to meet, and gave the public a reason to come and find out what it does.
> Because the most affordable hospital bill is the one that never has to be shared.

heydoc.t: We Kongsi x HEYDOC Health: Bringing Outpatient Care Closer to Our Members
heydoc.d: A partnership that extends healthcare support beyond hospitalisation, giving WeShare members access to outpatient healthcare services through the Conditional Outpatient Benefit.
heydoc.alt: The We Kongsi and HEYDOC Health partnership signing ceremony, 18 May 2026
body: On 18 May 2026, We Kongsi partnered with HEYDOC Health to strengthen the healthcare support available to its members. The partnership agreement between Kita Kongsi Sdn Bhd and HEYDOC Health Sdn Bhd was signed at a ceremony marking a strategic healthcare collaboration between the two organisations.
The agreement was signed by **Tan Chun Sian**, Chief Executive Officer of We Kongsi, and **Dr Raymond Choy**, Chief Executive Officer of HEYDOC Health.

The collaboration marked an important step in the development of We Kongsi's healthcare ecosystem, extending its services beyond hospitalisation cost-sharing and into everyday outpatient care. Through this partnership, HEYDOC Health became the healthcare service provider powering the **Conditional Outpatient Benefit (COB)**, an optional add-on available to WeShare members.
## Addressing the Healthcare Needs Beyond Hospitalisation
Hospitalisation is often associated with significant medical expenses, and it is what a community cost-sharing programme is built for. But healthcare needs do not begin and end in a hospital ward.

A persistent cough, a fever, a sore throat or stomach discomfort may not require hospital admission, yet these conditions still deserve timely medical attention. Members need convenient ways to consult a doctor, receive medical advice and access appropriate treatment without unnecessary delays.

This is where the partnership with HEYDOC Health plays an important role. By introducing the Conditional Outpatient Benefit, We Kongsi provides eligible WeShare members with an additional way to access outpatient healthcare services, complementing the programme's existing focus on hospitalisation cost-sharing.
## How HEYDOC Health Powers the Conditional Outpatient Benefit
HEYDOC Health supports the delivery of the COB by providing access to outpatient healthcare services through its healthcare network and digital healthcare capabilities.
Depending on the member's eligibility and the applicable benefit conditions, the services include:
- **Online doctor consultations:** Members can consult licensed doctors through teleconsultation, without having to travel to a clinic for every medical concern.
- **Access to outpatient care:** Eligible members can visit participating healthcare providers on the MiCare GP panel, which covers 4,709 clinics across 663 towns and cities.
- **Medication support:** Where clinically appropriate and subject to the applicable arrangements, members can receive medication through the available pharmacy services.
Teleconsultation is available daily from 9:00am to 10:00pm. Medication delivery arrangements are subject to the daily cut-off time and availability.
The benefit supports up to RM120 per episode, across eight episodes a year, for 17 eligible outpatient conditions. It is available from RM15 a month and begins after the 90-day waiting period.
## Two Organisations, Complementary Roles
The partnership brings together two organisations with different but complementary responsibilities.

**We Kongsi** administers the medical cost-sharing programme and makes the Conditional Outpatient Benefit available as an optional add-on to eligible WeShare members. **HEYDOC Health** provides the healthcare service infrastructure and supports the delivery of outpatient services under the COB.

This arrangement reflects how the wider programme is organised. The administrators who assess a hospitalisation, the licensed trustee who holds the Sharing Account, the actuaries who review the model and the Shariah advisory who certify it are each independent organisations with a single responsibility. Each focuses on its own role while working towards a shared objective: making healthcare support more accessible to the community.
## What This Means for WeShare Members

For WeShare members who choose to participate in the COB, the partnership offers an additional avenue for outpatient healthcare support. It means members can access healthcare services for eligible outpatient conditions, rather than relying solely on hospital-based support when medical needs arise.

Two points are worth stating clearly. The COB is an **optional add-on**, not a benefit included automatically in every WeShare membership, and it cannot be taken up without a WeShare membership. And using it does not affect the hospitalisation cost-sharing: an outpatient episode has no effect on a member's monthly sharing contribution or on the Sharing Account.
## Building a More Connected Healthcare Ecosystem

The collaboration with HEYDOC Health represents more than a service partnership. It reflects We Kongsi's continued effort to build a healthcare ecosystem that responds to different stages of a member's healthcare journey.

Most of a member's healthcare year is made up of small, ordinary needs, with the occasional serious one. By combining community-based hospitalisation cost-sharing with access to outpatient services through the COB, We Kongsi continues to explore ways to make healthcare support more accessible, practical and connected.
> Because supporting one another in healthcare should go beyond the hospital doors.

shariah.t: We Kongsi Receives Shariah Compliance Certification
shariah.d: An independent review by Afsha Shariah Advisory of how the programme operates — published in full, so it can be read rather than taken on trust.
shariah.alt: The Shariah Compliance Certificate issued by Afsha Shariah Advisory
body: Afsha Shariah Advisory Sdn. Bhd., acting as Shariah Advisor to Kita Kongsi Sdn. Bhd., reviewed the We Kongsi Program and certified it as Shariah-compliant.
## Why an Independent Review Matters
This is not a claim We Kongsi makes about itself, and that distinction is where the value of the certificate lies.

Afsha is an external advisory firm. The review is theirs, the assessment is theirs, and the certification is theirs to grant or to withhold. An organisation declaring its own product compliant is making a marketing statement. An organisation submitting it for independent assessment is doing something different.
## What Was Reviewed
The review examined how the programme actually operates, rather than how it is described:
- **How members contribute** — the membership fee, the monthly sharing contribution, and the relationship between the two.
- **Where the funds are held** — a member-owned Sharing Account, held and managed by a licensed trustee, which We Kongsi has no access to.
- **How a case is settled** — assessment by an independent third-party administrator against the published Program Guidelines, before anything is shared.

That is the appropriate scope for a review of this kind. The principles of mutual aid are not demonstrated by a mission statement. They are demonstrated by where the funds are held and who decides how they are used.
## What Shariah Compliance Means Here
In practice, it describes a structure built on mutual aid and community solidarity: members contributing to help one another with medical costs, rather than purchasing an undertaking from a company.

This is why the structural elements above are the ones under review. Funds held separately from the operator, decisions made by parties with no interest in the outcome, and an arithmetic published in full each month are not incidental features of the programme. They are what the compliance consists of.
## The Certificate Itself
The certificate carries number **CF/003/2026/03**, is dated **8 January 2026** and is valid until **7 January 2027**, subject to review by the relevant authorities and by Afsha Shariah Advisory.

It is published in full on the We Kongsi home page — not as a badge or a summary, but as the document itself, with its number and dates legible, so that members can confirm the position for themselves.
## The Limits of a Certificate
Two points are worth stating plainly.

A certificate applies to the programme, not to any individual medical decision. Whether a particular case is approved is determined by the Program Guidelines and the independent administrator who applies them.

A certificate also has a period. One valid to a stated date must be renewed to carry weight beyond it, which is why the dates are printed on the certificate and the certificate is published rather than described.
## Shariah-Compliant, and Open to Everyone
One point is worth repeating, because it is the most common misunderstanding.
Shariah compliance describes **how the programme is built**. It is not a condition of membership. We Kongsi is open to Malaysians of any religion or background, and always has been.
> Because an assurance is only meaningful when someone independent gives it, and anyone can read the document.

mantap.t: "We Kongsi Mantap!" — A Member Family's Experience
mantap.d: A member family on what being part of the community has meant to them — in their own words, on their own video.
body: The clearest account of what this programme does comes from the members it has supported. This one is theirs rather than ours.
## Recorded by Members, Not by Us
Members record these videos themselves and publish them on the We Kongsi channel. There is no script, and the ones that appear on this site are the ones members have chosen to make public.
They tend to cover the same three things, in the same order: the bill that arrived, the support the community provided, and what it meant not to face it alone.
## Why a Video Rather Than a Written Quote
A written testimonial can always be improved — edited for clarity, shortened, adjusted to sound a little more polished. Each of those improvements also makes it slightly less a member's own account.
A video is harder to adjust in that way. A viewer can judge for themselves whether a member means what they are saying, and that matters for a programme whose case rests on being verifiable.
## Consent Comes First
A medical experience is a private matter. It involves a diagnosis, a hospital stay and a household's finances, and none of that becomes public simply because the household is a member.

Nothing is published here without the member deciding to publish it. That is why this page carries fewer stories than there are cases in the sharing reports. The difference between those two numbers is members who would prefer not to share their experience publicly, which is entirely their decision.
## One Account Among Many

Every figure in a monthly sharing report represents a difficult period for a real household. Since September 2023 the community has supported hundreds of approved cases, each one a line in a published document and a serious event for the family behind it.
This family's video is one of those lines, told by the people who lived through it.
> Because the people best placed to explain what this community does are the ones it has supported.

anniversary.t: Three Years of We Kongsi: Celebrating the People Behind the Mission
anniversary.d: The third anniversary dinner, marking three years of members, agents, partners and team building the community together.
anniversary.alt: The We Kongsi third anniversary dinner
body: On 18 April 2026, members, agents, partners and the We Kongsi team gathered for the programme's third anniversary dinner — an evening to mark three years of a community that has grown steadily since it began.
## Measuring Three Years Properly
A community programme can mark an anniversary in two ways. It can count how long it has existed, or it can count how many times it has done the thing it exists to do.

We Kongsi has shared medical costs every month since September 2023. Each of those months has been published in full: the number of approved cases, the total medical cost approved, the number of active members who shared it, the amount each of them contributed, and the balance carried forward to the next period.
That unbroken record of monthly reports is what the evening was really marking.
## The People in the Room
The anniversary dinner is one of the few occasions when every part of the programme is together in one place.
- **Members**, including those the community has supported through a hospital admission, and those who have contributed for years without ever needing to call on it.
- **Agents**, who introduce and explain the programme within their own communities and are usually the first person a member contacts.
- **Partners**, the independent organisations that assess cases, hold the member-owned funds and review the model.
- **The team**, who spend most of the year supporting members by phone, message and email.

Those four groups rarely meet, and there is value in them doing so. A member who has only seen a monthly figure can meet the people behind it, and an agent who has answered the same question many times can hear how the answer has landed.
## What Three Years Demonstrates
The question the programme is asked most often is some version of: does it hold together over time?

A community medical cost-sharing programme works only if people continue to support one another — through quiet months when little is asked of them, and through heavy months when the sharing cap applies and the balance carries forward. That cannot be demonstrated in advance. It can only be built up, month by month.
Three years of published sharing reports is what that record looks like.
## And What It Does Not
A track record is evidence rather than a guarantee. Three years of published months shows that the model has held under the conditions it has met so far.

The appropriate response is to continue publishing every month, keep cases independently assessed and keep the actuarial review rigorous, rather than to treat an anniversary as the argument in itself. The next three years have to be built the same way as the first three.
> Because a community is not measured by how long it has existed, but by how often it has shown up.

network.t: Building a Stronger Healthcare Network Through Partnerships
network.d: We Kongsi does not run hospitals or clinics. It works with the organisations that do — and the reach of those panels is the practical measure of a membership.
network.alt: A member being seen at the reception counter of a panel clinic
body: A medical cost-sharing programme is only as useful as the places where its members can be seen. Financial support that arrives after the fact is a reimbursement; what a member needs at an admissions counter is a hospital that already recognises them.

That is the purpose of a healthcare panel, and it is why two of We Kongsi's most important partnerships are not with individual hospitals or clinics, but with the administrators who manage the networks of them.
## For Hospitalisation: The e-MAS Panel

Inpatient care is supported through the e-MAS panel, which covers **299 private and government hospitals across 16 states and territories**. e-MAS is an independent administrator, separate from We Kongsi, and it manages everything that happens between a member arriving at a hospital and the approved costs being settled.
- **At the admissions counter:** the member presents their We Kongsi and e-MAS membership details, and the hospital verifies eligibility directly with e-MAS.
- **For eligible admissions:** e-MAS issues a Guarantee Letter to the hospital, confirming the approved scope of medical cost-sharing support.
- **On settlement:** approved costs are settled between e-MAS and the hospital directly, so the member does not need to pay the full bill upfront. Any applicable co-share portion still applies.
- **Before a planned admission:** the e-MAS careline on 03-9213 0103 can confirm a hospital's panel status and answer Guarantee Letter enquiries.
The Guarantee Letter is the most practical part of this arrangement. It is what allows a family to focus on treatment rather than on finding a large sum at short notice.
## For Everyday Care: The MiCare GP Panel

Outpatient care is supported through the MiCare GP panel, which covers **4,709 clinics across 663 towns and cities**. This is the network behind WeCare and behind the WeShare outpatient add-on, and MiCare is the careline to contact for anything relating to a clinic visit, on 1800 88 7940.

The spread of the panel matters as much as its size. A large network concentrated in a few major cities would serve members less well than one that reaches the towns where they actually live, which is why the clinic directory on this site is organised by state and town rather than presented as a single list.
## Why the Programme Is Structured This Way

We Kongsi could have contracted hospitals and clinics directly. It does not, for the same reason it does not hold members' funds or assess its own cases: the organisation administering a programme should not also be the one verifying it.

e-MAS verifies admissions and settles approved costs. MiCare manages the clinic network. A licensed trustee holds the member-owned Sharing Account. Independent actuaries review the model. Each organisation is accountable for its own part, and that separation is what makes the programme verifiable rather than simply promised.
## Panel Lists Change, and That Matters

Hospitals and clinics join and leave panels over time. The directories on this site state the month they reflect — the e-MAS private panel of September 2026, the government panel of June 2026, and the MiCare GP panel of September 2026 — and they are a starting point rather than a guarantee.
Before any planned admission or clinic visit, members should confirm the current status with the relevant careline. It takes a few minutes, and it avoids an avoidable complication on a difficult day.
> Because a healthcare network is measured by whether a member can be seen, close to home, on the day they need it.

family.t: A Family Trip That Took a Turn
family.d: A daughter admitted for two to three days after a trip to Kuala Lumpur, and a bill of around RM2,200 the family had not planned for.
body: A family trip to Kuala Lumpur ended at a hospital admissions counter when the member's daughter developed stomach problems serious enough to require admission. She was in hospital for two to three days.
The total bill came to around RM2,200 — an amount the family had not budgeted for, and had no way of anticipating.
## In the Member's Own Words

" "After our family trip to KL, my daughter had to be admitted to the hospital for 2–3 days because of stomach problems. The bill came to around RM2,200, which was an unexpected expense for our family. Thank goodness I had We Kongsi to help ease the burden during that time."
## The Bills That Rarely Make the Headlines

RM2,200 is not a catastrophic figure, and it is not the kind of amount that forces a family to sell anything. It belongs to a different category: the unexpected expense that quietly reorganises a household's month.

Most families could find RM2,200 if they had to, but usually at the cost of something else — a repair postponed, school expenses rearranged, savings set aside for another purpose. These are the medical costs that affect the greatest number of households, and they are a large part of what the community shares each month.

Larger admissions do occur, and they are why the annual medical cost-sharing limit is RM1,000,000. But each monthly sharing report publishes the number of approved cases alongside the total approved cost, so members can see for themselves what a typical case looks like.
## How the Support Worked
The process is the same regardless of the size of the bill.
- **At the admissions counter**, the hospital verified the member's eligibility with e-MAS.
- **For the eligible admission**, e-MAS issued a Guarantee Letter to the hospital.
- **Approved costs** were settled between e-MAS and the hospital directly, so the family did not need to pay the full amount upfront and claim it back afterwards.
The approved portion then entered that period's sharing report, divided across every active member and capped at RM60 per member.
## Being Seen Away From Home
One detail is worth drawing out, because it is rarely considered until it matters. A membership is not tied to the town it was taken out in.

The e-MAS panel covers 299 hospitals across 16 states and territories, and the MiCare GP panel covers 4,709 clinics in 663 towns and cities. That coverage is most valuable precisely when something goes wrong somewhere unfamiliar — on a trip, at work away from home, or while visiting family.
> Because a medical bill does not have to be large to be the most difficult thing a family faces that month.

king.t: When Heart Pain Led to an Unexpected Admission
king.d: King Khairul was admitted after experiencing heart pain, with a total medical bill of around RM60,000.
king.alt: King Khairul, a We Kongsi member
body: King Khairul was admitted to hospital after experiencing heart pain. It was not something he had any reason to anticipate, and the total medical bill came to around RM60,000.
## In His Own Words

" "I was admitted to the hospital after experiencing heart pain, and it was something I never expected to happen to me. My total medical bill came to around RM60,000. I'm truly grateful to have had We Kongsi and the support of the community when I needed it most."
## Why a Figure Like This Matters
Two characteristics make a medical bill genuinely difficult to manage, and a cardiac admission has both.
- **The size.** RM60,000 is beyond what most Malaysian households hold in reserve. It is not a matter of adjusting a monthly budget.
- **The timing.** It arrives without notice. There is no opportunity to prepare, no instalment plan agreed in advance, and no option to postpone treatment to a more convenient time.
Together, these turn a health problem into a financial one — and the financial consequences often continue long after the medical treatment has ended.
## How the Community Responds

This is the central purpose of the model. The approved portion of an admission is divided across every active member for that sharing period, and no member contributes more than RM60 in a month, however heavy the month has been. Any amount above the cap is carried forward across the community rather than charged to anyone.
Several thousand members each contribute an amount they can comfortably manage. One member avoids losing many years of savings. That is the whole arrangement, and it is why the programme exists.
## Why the Annual Limit Is Set Where It Is
WeShare's medical cost-sharing limit is RM1,000,000 a year. In an ordinary month that figure can look like a marketing number.

It is not. It is there for admissions that do not stop at RM60,000 — those involving complications, a second procedure, or a stay of several weeks. A limit only matters on the day it is tested, and the members it is written for are usually those who never expected to test it.
## Support, and What It Means at the Time
The closing line of King's own account is worth re-reading: grateful for the support of the community **when I needed it most**.

A Guarantee Letter at an admissions counter is a practical, financial arrangement. On the day itself, it is also what allows a member to concentrate on their treatment rather than on how the bill will be met.
> Because nobody should have to face a bill of that size alone, or find it within a week.

albari.t: An Unexpected Accident on the Way to Work
albari.d: Three years a member before he needed the community himself. An accident on the way to work left Muhammad Al-Bari with broken bones and bills of around RM82,000.
albari.alt: Muhammad Al-Bari, a We Kongsi member
body: Muhammad Al-Bari joined We Kongsi three years before he ever needed it. For three years he contributed each month towards other members' medical costs, without once calling on the community himself.
Then, on an ordinary morning on the way to work, he was involved in an accident that resulted in broken bones, with medical expenses reaching around RM82,000.
## In His Own Words

" "I have been a We Kongsi member for three years, and I never expected that one day I would need the support myself. On my way to work, I was involved in an accident that resulted in broken bones, with medical expenses reaching around RM82,000. Knowing that I had We Kongsi gave me peace of mind during my recovery."
## What a Figure Like RM82,000 Represents

Orthopaedic admissions tend to be costly in a particular way. They rarely involve a single procedure and a single night. More often it is surgery, implants, imaging and an extended stay, followed by a recovery that continues to carry costs after discharge.

A household facing RM82,000 does not usually lose everything. What it loses is the next several years of plans — a deposit saved for, a course of study, a business about to begin. The bill is met in the end, but it is met out of a future that was intended for something else.
## Accidental Injury Does Not Wait

Most support under WeShare begins after a waiting period: 90 days for common illness and 180 days for specified illnesses. The reason is the same one that applies to any mutual arrangement. Without a waiting period, people would join on the way to hospital, and the community would be asked to carry costs it had no opportunity to prepare for.

Accidental injury is the exception. **It is eligible from the day a membership begins, up to RM10,000**, because an accident is not something anyone can plan around. The remainder of an admission such as this follows the ordinary sharing rules.
## Three Years of Contributing, and One Morning
This is the pattern behind most member stories, and it is easy to overlook.

A member contributes month after month towards people they have never met. There is no event and no claim — only a regular payment that may seem, for a long time, to do nothing. Then one day, without warning, the position is reversed, and several thousand members quietly share a cost that no single household could have absorbed.
Those three uneventful years were not Al-Bari waiting for his turn. They were Al-Bari being part of somebody else's.
> Because for three years he was the support, and then one morning he was the one who needed it.

honey.t: A RM45,000 Surgery and the Support of the Community
honey.d: Honey, 27, from Perak, on moving away from expensive medical insurance — and what happened when she needed a RM45,000 surgery.
honey.alt: Honey, a We Kongsi member from Perak
body: Honey is 27 and from Perak. Before joining We Kongsi she had been paying for medical insurance, and the cost of the premiums was what led her to look for an alternative.
It is a decision many people in their twenties are weighing up, often without much information to go on. Some time after making it, she needed surgery costing RM45,000.
## In Her Own Words

" "After switching from expensive medical insurance, I found We Kongsi to be much more affordable. When I underwent a RM45,000 surgery, the support I received gave me and my family real peace of mind."
## What She Moved To
It is important to be precise here, because an accurate description is more useful to a reader than a flattering one.

We Kongsi is **not insurance and not Takaful**. Nothing is underwritten, there is no sum insured, and no company undertakes to pay. It is a community of members who agree to share one another's approved medical costs, month by month, under published guidelines.
What supports that agreement is structural rather than contractual:
- **The funds are not held by We Kongsi.** They sit in a member-owned Sharing Account held and managed by a licensed trustee.
- **The decisions are not made by We Kongsi.** Every case is assessed against the published Program Guidelines by an independent third-party administrator.
- **The arithmetic is not private.** Each month's approved total, active member count and per-member share is published in full.
## An Honest Comparison
A reader weighing the same decision deserves both sides of it.

What a member gives up is a contract of indemnity — a regulated insurer's undertaking, backed by capital, that a defined sum will be paid. What a member gains is a lower monthly cost, a monthly sharing contribution capped at RM60, and a mechanism that can be read and checked end to end.
Neither is automatically the better choice for everybody. They are different arrangements, and anyone moving between them should understand clearly which one they hold.
## Her Own Account

Honey recorded her own testimonial, and it is published on the We Kongsi channel. It is a few minutes long and worth watching for anyone currently reviewing a renewal notice and considering the alternatives.
These stories are published in members' own words rather than written on their behalf, because a member's own account of their experience is the most reliable one available.
> Because peace of mind is only ever tested on the day it is needed.

xinmin.t: A RM15,000 Surgery: Support When It Matters Most
xinmin.d: Xin Min, 19, from Perak, on the surgery she needed and what the cost would have meant for her family.
xinmin.alt: Xin Min, a We Kongsi member from Perak
body: Xin Min is 19 and from Perak. At that age most people have not given much thought to hospital bills, which is understandable and also part of what makes an unexpected one difficult.
She required surgery costing RM15,000.
## In Her Own Words

" "The RM15,000 surgery I needed would have been a huge burden for my family. Thanks to We Kongsi and the support of the community, I was able to focus on my recovery instead of worrying about the medical expenses."
## What the Support Actually Provided
It is worth noticing where that account ends. Not on the figure, but on what the figure allowed her to stop thinking about.

The financial support matters. What it provides during the week it is needed is the ability to concentrate on recovery rather than on how the cost will be met. A nineteen-year-old recovering from surgery has one responsibility, and calculating her family's finances is not it.
## Why Younger Members Are Part of the Community

A cost-sharing community depends on members who are statistically less likely to need it. That is not a cynical observation; it is simply how the arithmetic works, and it is the same arithmetic that means a nineteen-year-old pays the same membership fee as everyone else.

The arrangement is reciprocal, and it is open about being reciprocal. In most months Xin Min's contribution supports a member much older than she is. In one month, several thousand members' contributions supported her.
## Why the Waiting Period Exists
Membership is open from age 5 to 45, and support begins after a waiting period: 90 days for common illness, 180 days for specified illnesses, and accidental injury from the first day.

Those periods are not an obstacle placed in a new member's way. They are what prevents the community from being joined on the way to hospital, and they are the reason a member who joins young, and contributes through years of needing nothing, is what makes the programme work for the member who does.
> Because the best time to join a community like this is long before you need it.

money.t: Where Does the Community's Money Go?
money.d: How eligible medical costs are reviewed, how each month's sharing amount is calculated, and why it is capped at RM60.
money.alt: An illustration of how community sharing works
body: The question members ask most frequently is also the most important one: where does my money actually go?
The answer has three parts, and what they have in common is that none of them involves We Kongsi holding the funds.
## First: There Are Two Separate Payments
This is the point that causes the most confusion, so it is worth separating before anything else.

- **The membership fee** — RM40 a month, RM100 a quarter or RM360 a year — funds the running of the programme: administration, the careline, case assessment and the platform. It is paid in advance and does not go towards medical cost-sharing.
- **The monthly sharing contribution** is separate. It varies from month to month, it is capped, and it is the amount that goes towards other members' approved medical costs.
One pays for the programme to operate. The other is the medical cost-sharing itself.
## Second: The Funds Are Held by a Licensed Trustee
Money set aside for sharing is held in a member-owned **Sharing Account**, managed by Palladium, a licensed trustee. We Kongsi has no access to it.

This is a structural safeguard rather than a courtesy. The organisation administering the programme cannot reach the funds, which means members' money does not depend on the continued good conduct of the administrator.
## Third: Cases Are Assessed Independently

When a member is admitted to hospital, an **independent third-party administrator** reviews the case against the published Program Guidelines before anything is shared. We Kongsi does not determine what the community supports.
Approved costs for the period are then divided across every active member — those who have completed the 90-day waiting period — which produces that month's per-member figure.
## Why the Sharing Cap Is Central

Whatever a month's approved total comes to, **no more than RM60 is shared from a member's Sharing Account**. Any amount above the cap is carried forward across the community rather than charged to anyone.

The cap is what makes the arrangement workable in practice. Without it, a heavy month for the community would become a heavy month for every member's household budget, and a model that asks families to absorb an unpredictable cost has recreated the problem it set out to solve.
With the cap in place, a member knows the maximum in advance. That is the difference between sharing a risk and simply passing it around.
## And All of It Is Published

Each month's approved total, active member count and per-member amount appears in the sharing report, and the full document is available to download on the Transparency page — every month since September 2023.
> Because members should not have to trust the arithmetic. They should be able to check it.

reports.t: Monthly Sharing Reports: Keeping Our Community Informed
reports.d: Every month since September 2023, published in full — what was approved, how many members shared it, and what was carried forward.
reports.alt: An illustration of the monthly sharing report
body: We Kongsi has published a sharing report every month since September 2023.
Not a summary and not a selected highlight, but the document itself, available to download, with the case listing behind the totals.
## What Each Report Contains
Every report sets out the same information, in the same order, so that one month can be compared with another directly:
- **Total members** and **active members** — those who have completed the 90-day waiting period and therefore take part in that month's sharing.
- **Approved hospitalisation cases** for the period, and the **total medical cost approved**.
- **Cost per active member before the cap** — the division as it falls, whatever the figure.
- **The sharing cap**, and the **total actually shared** by members.
- **The balance carried forward** to the next period.
## The Sharing Period and How Reports Are Named

A sharing period runs from the 7th of one month to the 6th of the next, and each report is named for the month in which the period ends. The November 2026 report therefore covers 7 October to 6 November 2026.
This appears to be a technical detail until a member tries to match a report against a bank statement, at which point it becomes the most important one.
## How to Read a Report Quickly
For members who want the essentials, two figures tell most of the story: the **cost per active member before the cap**, and the **cap** itself.

Where the first is below the second, it was an ordinary month and members shared the amount the arithmetic produced. Where it is above, the month was heavy, the cap applied, and the difference was carried forward across the community rather than charged to households. That single comparison says more about a month than the headline total does.
## Designed to Be Verified
The arithmetic in a sharing report is published so that it can be checked:
- Active members multiplied by the per-member share equals the total shared.
- The difference between that figure and the approved cost is the amount carried forward.
Both calculations can be carried out by any member with the document in front of them.
## An Ongoing Record

Every report is available on the Transparency page, with a selector for each month published. The most recent month leads, and the full archive remains available — including the quiet months and the heavy ones in which the cap applied.
The heavy months are the most informative. Any programme can publish a favourable one.
> Because transparency that cannot be checked is only a claim.

wecare.t: Introducing WeCare: Everyday Outpatient Healthcare Made Simple
wecare.d: A standalone outpatient subscription — unlimited teleconsultations, panel clinic visits and medication support, with no waiting period. Launched 1 November 2026.
wecare.alt: Introducing WeCare — a standalone outpatient plan from We Kongsi
body: WeCare launched on 1 November 2026. It is a standalone outpatient healthcare subscription: a plan in its own right rather than part of WeShare, and available without membership of the hospitalisation cost-sharing community.
## What a Subscription Includes
- **Unlimited video consultations** with a licensed doctor, daily from 9:00am to 10:00pm including weekends and public holidays, at no additional cost.
- **Care Episodes** — two released each quarter, eight across a subscription year. One covers medication; one covers a visit to a panel GP clinic.
- **A panel of 4,709 clinics** across 663 towns and cities, on the MiCare GP network.
Care is delivered through the MiCare MyMed app by HEYDOC Health's network of licensed practitioners, clinics and pharmacies.
## How a Care Episode Works
Each Care Episode is supported up to **RM40**. Where the cost exceeds that, the member pays the difference and is told the amount before anything is charged.

One rule is particularly important: **a consultation never uses an episode.** Talking to a doctor is unlimited and free. An episode is only used when a member is actually treated — when medication is dispensed, or a clinic visit takes place.

That design is deliberate. A plan that charged for the consultation would encourage members to wait until they were certain something was wrong, and waiting is often how a minor condition becomes a hospital admission.
## No Waiting Period and No Health Declaration
WeCare begins on the day it is paid for. There is no waiting period, no health declaration, and no registration or administration fee.

The subscription costs RM45 a quarter or RM160 a year. It is paid in advance and is non-refundable. A member may cancel at any time, with no notice and no charge, and remains covered for the period already paid for. Restarting later costs RM30 in addition to the new subscription.
## What WeCare Is Not
Being precise about this is more useful to a prospective member than describing it favourably.

WeCare is a **paid outpatient healthcare subscription — not insurance, not Takaful and not a medical card**. Nothing is underwritten and no sum is insured. We Kongsi distributes and administers the plan; the care itself is delivered by licensed practitioners through the panel network.

WeCare also does not cover hospitalisation. A member who wants hospital costs shared by the community needs WeShare. WeCare is designed for the far more frequent, everyday healthcare needs that do not involve a hospital.
The full terms, including the 21 common acute conditions the plan supports, are set out in the WeCare Program Guidelines.
> Because most of a healthcare year is made up of small, ordinary needs — and those deserve support too.

cob.d: The optional outpatient add-on for WeShare members — what it supports, what it costs, when it begins, and how it differs from WeCare.
cob.alt: A member consulting a doctor by video call
body: The Conditional Outpatient Benefit is an optional add-on to a WeShare membership, available from **RM15 a month** and beginning after a 90-day waiting period.
It is not a standalone plan. It cannot be taken up without a WeShare membership, and it is not included automatically in one.
## What the Benefit Provides
- **Eight care episodes a year** — two on activation, followed by two more each quarter.
- **Up to RM120 of support per episode**, across telemedicine and a visit to a panel clinic.
- **Unlimited supplementary teleconsultations** with a licensed doctor, daily from 9:00am to 10:00pm.
- **17 eligible outpatient conditions**, listed in the Program Guidelines.
Telemedicine is delivered by HEYDOC Health, and clinic visits take place at MiCare panel clinics nationwide.
## How a Member Uses It
A member begins with a teleconsultation, describing the problem to a licensed doctor. For many everyday conditions, that is sufficient.

Where more is required, a visit to a panel clinic is arranged. And where hospital care is needed, the doctor refers the member to a panel hospital, at which point the hospitalisation side of WeShare applies. In that sense the outpatient benefit is doing its most valuable work: getting a member in front of a clinician early enough for a referral rather than an emergency.
## COB and WeCare: The Difference
COB and WeCare provide similar services and are frequently confused with one another. The distinction is straightforward:
- **COB is an add-on to WeShare.** The member already shares hospitalisation costs with the community and is adding everyday outpatient care to that membership.
- **WeCare is a standalone subscription.** The subscriber wants outpatient care without being part of the hospitalisation cost-sharing community.
A WeShare member adds COB. Someone who wants outpatient support without hospitalisation cost-sharing subscribes to WeCare. There is no need for both.
## It Does Not Affect the Hospitalisation Sharing
This is the question asked most often about the COB, and the answer is clear: **using the outpatient benefit has no effect on the hospitalisation cost-sharing.**

An outpatient episode does not change a member's monthly sharing contribution, is not drawn from the Sharing Account, and does not count towards the RM1,000,000 annual medical cost-sharing limit. The two operate alongside one another.
## Why the Benefit Begins on Day 90

COB begins after the same 90-day waiting period that applies to common illness under WeShare. This is not an arbitrary delay. A benefit with no waiting period would be taken up on the way to a clinic, and that cost would fall on the rest of the community.
The full terms are set out in the We Kongsi Program Guidelines.
> Because one membership should answer both kinds of day: the hospital admission, and everything that comes before it.

whatsnew.d: The current entry age for new members, who can open an account, when support begins, and the latest programme updates.
body: This is a regular update on changes to the We Kongsi Program Guidelines, membership procedures, eligibility and healthcare services. It sets out where things stand as of November 2026.
## Entry Age for New Members: 5 to 45
The entry age for new members is **5 to 45 years**, counted on the day of enrolment.

This applies to each individual enrolled as a member, including family members enrolled under an account. A member who joins within that range remains a member as they grow older; the limit applies at the point of enrolment, not afterwards.
## Who Can Open an Account, and Who Can Be Enrolled
These are two different things, and the distinction matters when a family joins together.
- **The account owner must be 18 or over.** The owner holds the membership account, enrols the members under it and manages them.
- **Members may be aged 5 to 45** at enrolment. A five-year-old can be a member, but cannot be an account owner.
- **Families can be enrolled together** under a single account, with the owner managing each member's membership.
## When Support Begins
Waiting periods are unchanged, and they are worth restating whenever eligibility is discussed:
- **Accidental injury** is eligible from the first day of membership, up to RM10,000.
- **Common illness** is eligible after 90 days.
- **Specified illnesses** are eligible after 180 days.

Waiting periods are what prevent the community from being joined at the point of needing it, and they are the reason members who contribute through years of needing nothing are able to rely on it when they do.
## WeCare Is Now Available

WeCare launched on 1 November 2026 as a standalone outpatient healthcare subscription — unlimited teleconsultations daily from 9:00am to 10:00pm, Care Episodes for medication and panel clinic visits, no waiting period and no health declaration.

It is separate from WeShare and from the Conditional Outpatient Benefit. A WeShare member who wants everyday outpatient care adds the COB; someone who wants outpatient care without hospitalisation cost-sharing subscribes to WeCare.
## The Latest Sharing Report
The November 2026 sharing report covers the period from 7 October to 6 November 2026. In that period, 53 hospitalisation cases were approved at a total medical cost of RM367,215.07.

With 6,078 active members, the sharing cap applied: each member shared RM60.00, for a total of RM364,680.00, and the balance of RM2,535.07 was carried forward to the next period. The full report is available to download on the Transparency page.
## Where to Confirm Anything Here

The Program Guidelines remain the authoritative source for eligibility, waiting periods, limits and procedures, and both documents are available on this site. For anything specific to an individual membership, the team can be reached on WhatsApp.
> Because members should hear about changes to their own programme from the programme itself.

arhuzaim.t: An Ordinary Day at Work, and a RM133,000 Hospital Bill
arhuzaim.d: More than three years a member before he ever needed it. A road accident put Mohd Arhuzaim bin Samijan in a private hospital, with treatment reaching RM133,000.
arhuzaim.alt: Mohd Arhuzaim bin Samijan at home with his wife, after the accident
body: Mohd Arhuzaim bin Samijan left for work the way he had left for work a thousand times before. There was nothing about that morning to mark it out as the one he would still be talking about afterwards.

A road accident sent him to a private hospital, where the treatment came to RM133,000. By then he had been a We Kongsi member for more than three years, contributing every month towards costs that had always belonged to somebody else.
## What a Figure Like RM133,000 Represents

Major trauma is expensive in a way that is difficult to picture until the itemised bill arrives. It is rarely one procedure. It is the emergency admission, the imaging, the surgery and whatever the surgery requires, the days in a ward that are charged by the day, and the follow-up that carries on after discharge.

At that size the question stops being whether a household can afford the treatment and becomes what it will have to give up to pay for it. Savings meant for something else, a vehicle, a property, help asked for from family — most people find the money somehow. What they do not get back is the years it took to put it together.
## From Admission to Discharge
The valuable part of his account is the ordinary part: what actually happens between arriving at a hospital and being allowed to leave it.
- **Getting in.** A member admitted to a panel hospital is assessed by e-MAS, the third-party administrator, which handles the Guarantee Letter. The member is not left to negotiate at a counter.

- **During the stay.** The administrator deals with the hospital directly. That is what a panel is for — the paperwork runs between two organisations that handle it every day, rather than across a hospital bed.
- **Afterwards.** The eligible amount enters that month's sharing, and the ordinary sharing rules decide the rest.
He walks through his own version of all of this in the video below, which is a better account of it than any summary.
## No Single Member Pays for an Admission
RM133,000 is what the treatment cost. What the community shares is the eligible portion of it, and whatever a month's admissions come to, no member is asked for more than the monthly cap.
That is the whole mechanism, and it is worth stating plainly: a cost far beyond one household is divided until it is small for everybody.
## Three Years of Paying for People He Never Met
For more than three years his contribution went towards admissions he never saw, for members he has never met. Nothing came back, because nothing was meant to. That is what the contribution is.
Then one morning the direction reversed, and several thousand strangers shared a cost he could not have carried on his own.
> Because the day you need the community is never the day you planned for.

rider.t: The Rider Who Thought It Would Never Happen to Him
rider.d: For a rider, the road is where the day's income is earned. One accident left him with a hospital bill of around RM93,000 — and a message for everyone still riding.
rider.alt: A We Kongsi member who rides for a living, at home during his recovery
body: He is a rider. The motorcycle is not a weekend thing — it is how the day's income is earned, every day, on the same roads as everybody else.

Like most people who spend their working life on the road, he had filed the possibility of an accident somewhere at the back of his mind. Then it happened, and the hospital bill came to around RM93,000.
## In His Own Words
" "Don't be too calculating about the monthly contribution. We never know when misfortune will come."
That is the whole of his advice to other riders, and it is worth sitting with, because it is not really advice about money.
## The Risk Was Always There

Nobody who rides for a living needs to be told the road is dangerous. They know. The knowledge simply stops being useful after a while, because you cannot do the job and also treat every trip as a near miss.
So the risk does not change. What changes is whether anything has been put in place for the day it lands.
## What a Bill Like That Does to a Household

RM93,000 is not absorbed. It is converted into something else — a loan, a sold vehicle, money asked for from family, years of saving pointed somewhere new. For a household whose income depends on somebody being physically able to ride, it also arrives at the worst possible moment.
That is what his message is aimed at. A monthly contribution is small enough to feel like something you could skip. A bill of that size is not small enough to be skipped by anyone.
## Why the Contribution Is Supposed to Feel Like Nothing
Most months a member pays and nothing happens. No admission, no event, nothing comes back. After long enough it can start to look like paying for something you are not using.

It is being used. It is being used by whoever was admitted that month — and the arithmetic only works because everyone who was not admitted kept paying anyway. Then a month comes when those two groups change places.
> Because nobody plans for the accident. They plan for the possibility of one.
